newsitem.title: USA: Jesse Jackson to consult on black English plan.
newsitem.headline: Jesse Jackson to consult on black English plan.

text.p: Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson said Friday he will meet with Oakland, Calif., school officials about their controversial plan to recognise Black English, also known as Ebonics, as a distinct language.

The meeting will take place Monday, Jackson said, and he will try to work with Oakland School Superintendent Carolyn Getridge and school board members "in their quest for some form of compensatory education."

The board this month called on the district to provide teacher and parent training in Black English language patterns, recognise Ebonics as distinct from standard English and help black students who use Ebonics to master standard English. The word Ebonics was derived from ebony and phonics.

Jackson, speaking from Chicago on a conference call with Getridge and reporters, said he understood Oakland's plan was primarily an effort to secure government funding often alloted to schools burdened with non-English speaking students.
The Clinton administration criticised Oakland's proposal this week and said it would refuse to grant special funding.
Both Jackson and Getridge tried to play down elements in the proposal, calling the plan a "bridge to literacy."

In an interview taped for Saturday's "Evans & Novak" programme on CNN, Jackson said, "My concern is that there's too much focus now on that language pattern ... and not focusing on the bridge of building from where we are to equal opportunity, affirmative action and that's where we really must go."

Jackson said he would argue for more government funding for children with poor language skills but saw Ebonics as "a language pattern, not a language." Millions of black students do not master English and end up dropping out of school and possibly landing in prison, he said.

"If you cannot read, you cannot reason, if you cannot reason, you cannot do math, or do computer, or compete," Jackson said, adding that youths able to memorise entire albums of rap music lyrics ought to be able to master English.
Jackson, who initially blasted the school board's plan as "an unacceptable surrender borderlining on disgrace," said Oakland school officials themselves were reinterpreting the proposal.

He compared Ebonics to teaching correct pronunciation and locution to students who speak in a Southern drawl or "hillbilly"-accented English. He said help was needed in teaching literacy in school systems where students were at risk.

A school spokesman welcomed Jackson's visit but Oakland's superintendent and other school officials insist their critics do not fully understood the Ebonics policy. The district said in a statement it will not teach Ebonics in place of standard English and is not trying to classify Ebonics-speaking black students as bilingual in order to "pilfer" federal funds.
